body:
Three fixes to the suite's own guards, on one branch because the expensive part of shipping here is the
suite run rather than the fix.

Closes #2784. Closes #2313. Closes #2671. Also touches #2599 and #2570, see below.

## What shipped

### #2784: point every signature-anchored source guard at its function by name

`propertyBody` needs its marker to run all the way to the opening brace, so a guard using it on a
function is pinned to that function's signature AS WRITTEN. Add a parameter, rename one, or merely
re-wrap the signature across two lines, and the marker matches nothing: `propertyBody` returns nil,
which the `?? ""` call sites read as an empty body every `contains` is false against, and which the
`Issue.record` call sites report as a failure unrelated to the rule. #2417 hit it over two QueueView
functions, #2524 hit it again over two more.

Two halves:

1. **The sweep.** Every marker anchored to a function moved to
   `SourceGuardHelper.bodyOfFunction(named:in:)`, which finds the declaration by name and walks the
   parameter list by paren depth. 51 call sites over 29 files: the 37 pinning a whole signature as a literal
   argument, the 8 pinning the tail of a wrapped one (the four #2784 names, plus `AppNoticeTests`,
   `QueueRenderDataGuardTests`, `ScoutStartGateTests` and `WatchGapLineOnScreenTests`, which the issue's
   count of four did not reach), and the 6 that reached `propertyBody` through a loop variable or from
   behind a comment, listed under the vacuities below. Every assertion is untouched. Each name was checked to be declared
   exactly once in the file its guard reads, so `bodyOfFunction` cannot pick a different overload.

2. **The guard that closes the class**, which is the half worth having.
   `SourceGuardMarkerIntegrityTests.noPropertyBodyMarkerIsAnchoredToAFunction` refuses a NEW marker of
   either shape. Derived from the suite rather than a list beside it, so a marker written next year is
   covered without anybody remembering. It tells a mid-signature anchor from a legitimate marker by
   PARENS: a mid-signature anchor closes a paren it never opened (`agentInputs: AgentInputs) -> some
   View {`) or opens with the tail of a signature (`async -> ReconcileSummary {`). A marker merely
   holding a balanced call, `.onChange(of: focus) {`, is left alone. `theClassifierKnowsEachShapeItNames`
   builds each of the shapes the classifier's own comment enumerates, so a documented outcome nobody
   constructs cannot sit unreachable while the guard looks tested (L151).

**And the scan now reads code, not prose.** Every marker in `SourceGuardMarkerIntegrityTests` is
captured from the guard file's comment-stripped source. That file's own comments quote the exact call
shapes its patterns look for, so without the strip a commented-out call, or one that only ever existed
as an example, is scanned as a live guard: reported stale when it matches nothing, or reported as a
mid-signature pin when it is not a pin at all. A matcher that reads comments fires on its own
documentation (L103, and it is one of the three failure modes in #2726).

**Three live vacuities found and fixed while doing this**, all of them guards that were passing while
asking nothing, and none of them visible to the suite as it stood.

1. `QueueInvalidationGuardTests` held `"private func focusOnLeads("` and `"private func navigateToLead("`
   in an array, both stopping at the opening PAREN. `propertyBody` counts braces from the marker with
   depth already at 1, so those started inside the signature and only balanced at the end of the whole
   type: the "body" was every line of QueueView after those two functions, and both assertions were
   answered by any `jumpTarget = ` anywhere in it (L70). Invisible to
   `everyPropertyBodyMarkerEndsAtItsOwnBrace` because a marker held in an array is not a literal
   argument to `propertyBody`.
2. `ClosingAPitchOutFromTheRowTests` pinned
   `"func reachedOutRow(_ pair: (prospect: Prospect, recipient: Recipient, next: Date),"`, which stops
   at a COMMA, mid-signature, with the same consequence: `row` was every line of QueueView below that
   function, and the two `#expect(row.contains(...))` assertions were answered by anything in it.
   Invisible for a different reason, and the one that justifies the comment strip: four lines of comment
   sit between `propertyBody(` and its literal, so the scan's `propertyBody\(\s*"` never matched the
   call at all. Reading the guard file's CODE is what surfaced it, on the first offline run of the new
   check.
3. In the second of those two tests the `#require`d body was bound to `row` and then never read, so the
   only thing it asserted was that the marker resolved. Spelled as `_ = try #require(...)` now, which is
   what it actually claims.

### #2313: check that a helper both test targets use lives in the shared folder

`mac/project.yml` gives each test target its own folder plus `TestSupport`, so a type declared in
`OvertureTests/` is not visible from `OvertureHostedTests/` at all. That is what makes the drift silent:
the second target cannot reference the helper, so whoever needs it there COPIES it, both copies compile,
and they answer identically until one is fixed. `SharedTestHelperGuardTests` fails on any type name
declared at top level in more than one of `OvertureTests/`, `OvertureHostedTests/` and `TestSupport/`,
naming every file that declares it and saying it belongs in `TestSupport/`.

Measured 2026-08-16: 1050 top-level types in `OvertureTests/`, 46 in `OvertureHostedTests/`, 10 in
`TestSupport/`, zero overlap of any kind. So this is a guard against the next one, and its detector is
exercised on a planted copy rather than only ever watched not to fire.

### #2671: fail on a nested copy inventory ignore region

Two nested `copy-inventory:ignore-start` markers cancel each other: the inner region's `ignore-end`
closes the outer one too, so everything between there and the outer end leaks into
`docs/copy-inventory.md`. `unclosedIgnoreRegion` is structurally unable to see it, because nesting leaves
the starts and the ends balanced. `SwiftSource.nestedIgnoreRegion(in:)` reports the offending LINE (the
two markers are routinely hundreds of lines apart, so "this file nests one somewhere" is not actionable),
and `CopyInventory.build` throws `Failure.nestedIgnoreRegion(file, line)` before the unclosed check, so a
nested region is not reported as a missing marker that is not missing (L11).

### One stale comment

`GenrePrecedenceTests.swift:139` said "#1664 is open on that sentence being read by Dan". #1664 is
closed: #1657 stopped the fit reason printing the raw genre code on 2026-08-08. Corrected. No test; it is
a comment.

## What did not ship

### #2599: close as superseded, not fixed

#2784 covers it in full. #2599 asked for the sweep of every guard pinned to a function signature and
positioned itself as the mechanical subset of #2543, which has since closed; #2784 is that sweep with the
residue measured and named, and it adds the guard that stops a new one being written. The sweep here is
all 51 rather than only #2784's four for a mechanical reason: the preventive guard cannot be green while
37 whole-signature pins remain, so the sweep is the guard's prerequisite rather than a second job. Not
closed from here.

### #2570: dropped, its premise does not survive measurement

The issue asks the copy inventory to fail when an entry is an expression rather than a sentence, and
proposes the rule "an interpolation whose contents hold a bracket or a colon". Measured against
`docs/copy-inventory.md` as it stands: that rule fires on **112 of the 1365 entries** (84 hold a function
call, 10 a subscript, 18 a ternary). It is a gate nobody could go green on, and one that fires on the
common case is switched off within a day (L93).

Narrower variants were measured and fail the same way, because the shipped copy really does compose this
way: `Plural.count(count, "show")`, `PrepStatus.duration(seconds

author: masarray
body:
## Fix
Native Connect previously stopped after reading only scalar bytes `0x00..0x3F`, so the controller had a safety cache but the editor stayed on its local/default values.

This ports the donor web/native sync sequence correctly:

`heartbeat 0x1C → handshake 0x3F → CMD 0x40 active-memory read 0x0000..0x03AA → hydrate editor → LIVE ON`

## What changed
- read the complete **0x03AB / 939-byte** active K500 memory in **0x3A / 58-byte blocks**, with the donor 35 ms inter-block pacing
- LIVE remains OFF until every block is checksum-valid and the snapshot has propagated
- emit full `activeMemoryReady` in addition to the scalar safety cache
- seed `K500Controller` mirrored Top Music fields from the snapshot before LIVE to prevent a one-field edit from overwriting neighbouring fields with stale defaults
- decode the donor scalar split (`+8` then `+9`) and compact 5-byte live PEQ representation
- hydrate Music, Mic A/B, Main, Surround, Center, Sub, Reverb and Echo EQ models
- hydrate master volumes, music key/input gains, mic values/dynamics, all output mixer/dynamics values, effect values, delays, startup limits, record levels, device preset names/current slot and BT/BLE names
- bind `SectionWorkspace` and `SystemWorkspace` to the hydrated native device snapshot without changing layout
- hydration uses sync methods that do **not** emit `stateEdited`, so loading the device cannot echo-write values back to hardware
- generalize already-verified PEQ live writes from Music to the other known K500 PEQ section IDs
- extend `--engine-self-test` with a synthetic 939-byte device snapshot and assert hydration produces zero edit/write signals

## Safety
No guessed hardware writes were added for controls whose native command is not verified. Full readback is performed before LIVE is enabled; a timeout or short block leaves LIVE OFF.

## Donor parity
Implementation follows `masarray/ktv-studio-mixer-pro` `readActiveDeviceMemory()` and `liveMemory.ts`: total `0x03AB`, block `0x3A`, 35 ms pacing, scalar split mapping, compact EQ decoding and current-device import.

Stage **A3** of the unified-LSP engine contract (admin#49) — **stacked on #96 (A2)**; retargets as the stack merges.

`options.parse.budget` (default off): the main rule loop invokes `onCheck(ctx)` every `checkEveryN` iterations; a `false` return cancels the parse with the new `cancel` error code (added to the generated error registry — `schema/error-codes.json` regenerated, drift gate green). In recovery mode a cancelled parse returns `{ value, errors }` with the cancel recorded, giving a language server partial results on cancellation.

Cost when off: one falsy test per loop iteration. The threading caveat from the admin#49 review is documented in `ts/doc/options.md`: the hook enforces deadlines/budgets on the parsing thread; in-flight cross-thread cancellation is achieved by `onCheck` reading a flag another thread sets (`SharedArrayBuffer` pattern, specified for the server in the plan's B4).

Suite: 349 pass (+5 in `ts/test/budget.test.js`); flags-off behaviour unchanged. Go parity scheduled for P2 and recorded in `go/doc/differences.md`.

## Summary

Two docs-only explorations.

- **0451 — SuperDoc: DOCX documents as an opt-in plugin over xNet's Yjs and change log.** Yes to SuperDoc v2, only as a dynamically loaded, AGPL-labelled plugin (0342 precedent): the editor is AGPL and the v2 engine `@superdoc/docx-engine` is proprietary/obfuscated with an AI-analysis clause; v2 owns its Y.Doc and speaks only y-websocket/Hocuspocus/Liveblocks (v1's external `{ydoc, provider}` seam is gone). Data model: `Docx` node = xNet Y.Doc + canonical `.docx` blob + `markdown` cache; collab via a loopback y-websocket provider mirroring into the `useNode` Y.Doc (hub room as fallback; upstream issue for an external-doc option); docx-native comments and tracked changes as truth, mirrored into inbox/References/audit; agent edits always tracked. Prereq: 0385's >1 MB blob drop.
- **0452 — How far to pluginize: the kernel, the shell, and the lift-out ladder.** Convert first-party features into plugins only where the conversion widens the public plugin API, measured by 0206's lift-out test and a workspace-plugin honesty test. What blocks documents/databases/chat/tasks/CRM today is one closed enum (`TAB_NODE_TYPES`) and one hard-coded list (`SURFACES`) plus `registerHostedViews` requiring the complete map. Build a `nodeTypes` + `surfaces` contribution point, then walk leaf-first: meetings → CRM/finance/analytics → dashboards/maps → chat/channels → databases → documents. Never plugins: kernel, shell, plugin system, protocol schemas — plugins are their subjects.

## 変更内容

| 場所 | 内容 |
| --- | --- |
| `src/types/storage.ts` | `NoteEvent.renderStaff`（省略時=自分の五線・戻すときはプロパティごと削除） |
| `src/utils/crossStaffUtils.ts`（新規） | 「イベント→実際に載せるパート番号」を決める純関数。フォールバック・ビームのグループ分けもここ |
| `src/utils/storage.ts` | 読込検証に型チェック（`'below' \| 'above' \| undefined` 以外は拒否） |
| `src/components/PianoSystemCanvas.tsx` | 載せる先のクレフで StaveNote を作る／preFormat より前に `setStave`／またぎ位置でビームを切る／描画方法の切替 |

### 既存実装の共用について

判定を1か所（`crossStaffUtils`）に集約し、描画側・storage の検証・テストがすべて同じ関数を呼ぶ形にしました。段1b の `resolveRenderStave`（座標の取り所の1本化）も同じ答えを使えます。「同じロジックの2枚目」を作らないための配置です。

## 設計時の想定と違った点（設計メモ §10-3 に追記済み）

VexFlow 5 の `Voice.draw(ctx, stave)` は描画の直前に**全音符の五線を引数の五線で上書き**します。設計メモ §2 の「stave 未設定の音符にだけ伝播する」保護規則が効くのは `preFormat` までで、描画時は無条件に上書きされるため、またぎ音符を含む声部だけ `Voice.draw` を使わず音符単位で `setContext → drawWithStyle` しています（`Voice.draw` から五線の上書きだけを外した手順）。またぎを含まない声部は従来どおり `Voice.draw` を通ります。

## 検証結果

- `npx vitest --run`（変更に関係するテスト: PianoSystemCanvas 系全55ファイル + moonlight 回帰 + storage + 新規2ファイル）: **293 + 122 件すべて緑**
- `npm run lint:ratchet`: **326 件（基準値ちょうど）**
- `npm run build`: 成功
- ブラウザ（dev サーバー :5173・worktree に一時エントリを置いて目視。確認後に削除・コミットしていません）:
  - またぎなしでは g#/3・c#/4 がト音記号の五線の下に加線つきで描かれる
  - `below` を付けると同じ2音がヘ音記号の五線へ移り、g#/3 は加線なし、左手1拍目と x が揃い、ビームはまたぎ位置で切れる
  - コンソールエラーなし

### 追加した受入テスト（設計メモ §6 の 1・2・3前半・5）

| ファイル | 何を固定したか |
| --- | --- |
| `src/utils/crossStaffUtils.test.ts` | フォールバック3種・またぎ有無の判定・ビームのグループ分け |
| `src/components/PianoSystemCanvasCrossStaff.test.tsx` | 不変条件1（またぎ未使用の譜面の符頭座標を実測固定）／2（再生スケジュールが renderStaff の有無で不変）／3前半（下の五線に加線なし・ヘ音記号で読んだ高さ・左手と同じ x・またぎ位置でビームが切れる）／5（無効な向き・単段編成で self 描画） |
| `src/utils/storage.test.ts` | 保存→読込で保持／未指定ならプロパティが生えない／不正値は保存時に拒否 |

## 自信の無い点・レビューで見てほしいところ

1. **またぎを含む連符の括弧・数字**: 壊れてはいませんが、**グループ全体をまたぐ幅の括弧が下の五線の下側**に描かれます（ブラウザで確認）。設計メモ §4-2 の「崩れる場合は draw しない経路へ落としてよい」に該当するか微妙だったため、この段では**自動で消していません**（市販譜の月光は数字なしで、運用者は #294 のトグルで既に消せるため）。既定で消すべきなら段1b で入れます

3. **段1b に残した範囲**: 当たり判定 rect・選択枠・弧の端点はまだパートの五線を見ているため、またぎ音符のクリック位置は描画位置に追従しません（設計メモ §4-3 の1本化は段1b）

author: gdaybrice
body:
### Summary

Closes #2087. A channel can render a live progress card for the work it dispatched, because `actions.requested` and `action.result` reach its handlers. It never sees what a subagent does: a child publishes on its own child-session stream, so a Slack card shows "triage" for a whole 20-minute run while the nested steps stay invisible.

`execution/subagent-adapter.ts` already forwards a selected set of child events up to the parent turn, which is why a child's OAuth prompt appears in the parent's Slack thread today. This extends that same path to the action lifecycle, narrowed to nested dispatch: `actions.requested` entries with kind `subagent-call` or `remote-agent-call`, and `action.result` when the result kind is `subagent-result`. The parent re-emits the event through its own channel, so channels need no change (Slack's default handler already labels a `subagent-call` with its subagent name) and nesting works at any depth, the same way authorization events already do.

A child's own tool calls are deliberately not forwarded. Each forward is a durable workflow step replayed at every hop, so an event born at depth `d` costs `d` steps, and a tool `action.result` carries the full tool output as arbitrary JSON. The dispatch-only filter is what keeps this bounded; it is a load-bearing constraint, not a UX preference.

The second commit is a refactor with no behavior change. The progress lane landed as a third near-identical way to move a child event upward, so it merges `subagent-authorization-event` and `subagent-progress-event` into one `subagent-forwarded-event` kind. Both had the same five fields and no consumer ever told them apart. `subagent-input-request` stays separate because it carries `childContinuationToken` and drives the proxy-request bookkeeping.

Reviewers may want to look at two things. First, whether the dispatch-only filter is the right scope. Second, a known interaction: Slack's and Linear's default `actions.requested` handlers read and clear `channel.state.pendingToolCallMessage`, which is parent state, so a forwarded child event can consume the parent's buffered narration and post it against the wrong action. #2087 covers this and the `subagent.event` wrapper that would fix it properly; that wrapper needs a public `ChannelEvents` key and is out of scope here.

One note on process. #2087 is triaged `p2` but still open for design agreement, so this PR has not been agreed on yet. I opened it to make the proposal concrete and easy to read, not to skip that step. If you prefer the `subagent.event` wrapper, or a different scope for the filter, I am happy to rework it or close this and wait. Please treat the code as a proposal.

### Validation

- `pnpm typecheck` (34/34), `pnpm exec oxlint` (0 errors), `pnpm guard:invariants`, `pnpm check:deps`, `pnpm docs:check`
- `pnpm test:unit` (6450 passed, 1 skipped), `pnpm test:integration` (642 passed)
- New unit tests cover the filtering and payload construction, a routing test covers the new inbox lane (a dropped lane is not caught by typecheck), and an integration test asserts a parent channel's `actions.requested` and `action.result` handlers actually fire and mutate adapter state across the durable boundary
- Not run locally: scenario and e2e suites (CI only), TUI smoke tests

### Checklist

- [ ] I linked an issue with prior discussion confirming this change is wanted — #2087 is linked and triaged, but no design agreement yet
- [x] I ran the relevant checks from `CONTRIBUTING.md`
- [x] I added tests and documentation where relevant
- [x] I added a changeset if this touches the published `eve` package
- [x] DCO sign-off passes for every commit (`git commit --signoff`)

body:
## What was wrong

`configuredBuzzActorIngressPolicy()` reads `process.env` — **this process's** environment, not the deployment's. `~/.agent-control-plane/agentcpd-launch.sh` exports `ACP_BUZZ_INGRESS_SECRET` and `ACP_BUZZ_ALLOWED_ACTORS` from Keychain service `com.agentcontrolplane.agentcpd` (its `optional_keychain_value` loop, line 79) before starting the daemon. So a capture run from an ordinary shell sees neither, even when the deployment holds both.

The message said **"are not configured"** — a claim about the deployment that this check has no standing to make.

## Why it mattered

A red that is not a statement about its subject is the same defect as a green that is not, and this one cost a day. The absence was read as the deployment having no ingress policy at all. I filed #559 on that premise, and the remedy under discussion was to install an allowlist — **beside the one already installed**. That is the #552 shape: a second copy of a thing created because the first was looked for in the wrong place.

The near-miss had a specific cause worth recording. `docs/HANDOFF-20260814.md:25` names Keychain `buzz-desktop` — correctly, for `BUZZ_PRIVATE_KEY`. The launcher reads the *policy* from a different service, `com.agentcontrolplane.agentcpd`. Checking the service the handoff named, and the plist, and finding nothing, looked like a complete answer. The launcher is where the sourcing is actually decided, and it was the file that settled it.

## The change

The message now states what was observed, names where the deployment keeps these values, and says to re-run under the launcher's environment.

Verified by reading `agentcpd-launch.sh:6-7` (`ACP_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE` vs `ACP_BUZZ_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE`) and its `optional_keychain_value` loop. `lint` / `terminology` / `typecheck` pass locally; CI run URL to follow.

author: korjavin
body:
Half 2 of **bd med-m391**. Half 1 (repo back to public so Portainer can fetch) is already resolved by the owner — this closes the silent-failure gap that let it go unnoticed for five days.

## The blind spot

Portainer answers a redeploy webhook `204` immediately and does the git fetch + `compose up` asynchronously. `deploy.yml`'s webhook step only checks that the backgrounded `curl` exited 0, so a stack that never redeployed is indistinguishable from one that did. Result: 2026-08-11 → 2026-08-16, every Deploy Application run green, production 43 commits behind.

## Fix

**`internal/cloudserver/router.go`** — serve the existing `GET /api/version` on the base domain too, not just account subdomains. Same handler, same `buildID`, no new endpoint and no second build-id source. It carries no account and no user data (it is the value already injected as `<meta name="medtracker-build-id">`), so CI can poll it with no account and no Portainer API key.

**`.github/workflows/deploy.yml`** — after the webhook step, poll `https://<base>/api/version` until it reports the build this run produced. ~5 minute bound, 10s interval, hard job failure with an actionable message on timeout.

## The build-id format trap (deviation from the obvious approach)

`/api/version` does **not** report the commit SHA. `buildIDFrom` (`internal/cloudserver/version.go:25`) lifts the asset fingerprint back out of the served `index.html` — the first `?v=<BUILD_TS>` it finds, where `BUILD_TS` is `date +%Y%m%d-%H%M` from the "Inject Git SHA and Timestamp" step. Comparing it to `github.sha` would fail forever, which is worse than no check.

So that step now gets `id: stamp` and exports `build_ts` as a step output, and the verification compares against that. Confirmed against `version.go` + `version_test.go` before implementing.

Known ceiling, marked with a `ponytail:` comment: `BUILD_TS` has minute resolution, so two deploys landing in the same wall-clock minute would be indistinguishable. Rare enough to accept rather than invent a second build-id source.

## ⚠️ Owner action required for this to actually arm

Set the **`CLOUD_BASE_DOMAIN` GitHub repository variable** (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → **Variables**, not Secrets) to `cloud.myhealthbot.ai`.

The domain is deliberately **not** hardcoded. With the variable unset the step prints a `::notice::` and exits 0 — forks and fresh clones still deploy, they just don't get the check. Documented in `docs/cloud-deployment.md` as step 4 of the Portainer stack setup, including the "leaving it unset leaves the blind spot open" warning.

## Verification

- `go build ./...` — clean
- `go test ./... -count=1` — full tree green
- `internal/cloudserver/router_test.go`: new case in the existing `TestRouter_HostVariants` table (per the bead: extend, don't add a parallel file) asserting the base domain returns `{"build_id":"dev"}` for `/api/version`. The table's existing per-case CSP assertions run over it too, so the strict `connect-src 'self'` on the base domain is covered — no CSP behavior changed.
- The polling script was exercised locally under `bash --noprofile --norc -eo pipefail` (the exact shell GitHub uses) against a local fixture server: **skip** when the var is unset (exit 0), **match** (exit 0), **mismatch** (exit 1 after timeout), **unreachable host** (exit 1 after timeout). All four behave.
- `codex review --base master` — no findings.

## Notes / deferrals

- Parses `build_id` with `sed`, not `jq`. `jq` is preinstalled on `ubuntu-latest`, but `sed` is one fewer assumed tool and let me actually test the loop on this box. The payload is a single-key object from Go's `json.Encoder`; the pattern tolerates whitespace anyway.
- `curl -f` + `pipefail` mean any HTTP/network error yields an empty `got`, i.e. "keep polling" — the loop fails on *timeout*, never on one flaky request.
- Untouched, as instructed: the webhook-firing logic and the deploy-branch force-push. Both work.
- Not attempted: verifying the container image tag via the Portainer API. That would need a Portainer API key in GH secrets; polling the app's own build id needs no new secret and proves more (the code is actually *serving*, not merely deployed).

Do not merge yet — draft pending owner setting the repo variable.

body:
Caught in review, **one step before this number reached an immutable demo video**.

## The overclaim

The generated line read "5 of 5 refusal traps declined correctly" and described them as cases where the system says nothing. That is true of **two**. The other three **return a value**:

| case | actually returns |
|---|---|
| `near_threshold` | `field_verification_first` |
| `unsustained_recovery` | `flow_above_minimum_unsustained` |
| `undated_right` | the right, left unplaced |

Each is correct behaviour. **None of them is silence.**

## The fix

Every case declares its **kind**. Two **refuse**, raising rather than answering. Three **withhold** the consequential act — an order, a suspension, a placement — while still reporting what they saw.

**The distinction is kept rather than smoothed away, because withholding is the better of the two behaviours.** A system that answers "field verification first" is more useful than one that goes silent. Silence is not a virtue, and a summary that flattened the two would have been selling the weaker property.

## Guards

Two, both mutation-killed:
- one fails if the two kinds collapse into one
- one fails on **the exact sentence that was wrong**, so reverting the fact sheet to the overclaim turns CI red

## Note

This is the fourth consecutive review round to find a real defect in work I had just declared finished. The pattern across all four is the same: I verified the shape of my own reasoning rather than the behaviour underneath it.

## Summary

Renames the library from `esp_wireguard` to `wireguard` now that it lives in the `esphome-libs` organisation, and points the metadata and docs at the new home.

- `library.json`: `name` is now `wireguard`, `repository.url` points at `https://github.com/esphome-libs/wireguard.git`, and a `homepage` field was added to match the other `esphome-libs` repos (`esp-hub75`, `esp-audio-libs`).

author: easymod0
body:
`test:notify` builds an absolute timeline — `TODAY` (2026-08-13) through `TODAY + 5` — and then reaches for the real clock once, because entries in the future are refused and the "already ticked off" case needs a date the API will accept. Nothing kept the two apart.

So "two days ago" walks into the fixture calendar for **six real dates a year**. Ticking the habit on a fixture day makes that day's delivery `done_today`: nothing is sent, no outcome is recorded, and the checks below read a `notify_status` row that was never written.

On 2026-08-17 `twoDaysAgo` was `2026-08-15`, which is `deliverOn(15, 500)`, so these three failed with the feature working perfectly:

- `a delivery failure is readable over the API`
- `a retryable one is not reported as permanent`
- `dated from when it started going wrong`

master was green on the 16th and red on the 17th, on a suite nobody had touched. It blocks `Backup round-trip (personal)` on every open PR (#124, #131, #133) and would clear by itself on the 21st — which is the worst shape for this: long enough to block everything, short enough to look like a flake and be re-run rather than read.

## The fix

The real-clock day is clamped to the day before the calendar starts. It is still a real *past* date whenever the clamp fires, because it only fires once the real today has reached the window.

Verified over a 25-day sweep of simulated real dates: **6 collisions before, 0 after**, and no future date picked at any point. Confirmed causally by moving the ticked day from `today-2` to `today-9` against unfixed code — 3 failures to 0.

The invariant gets its own named check, so a future edit that moves the calendar fails on the thing that is actually wrong rather than as three confusing assertions about a delivery status two screens further down.

body:
## Summary

- **Foundation for #740, no behavior change.** Prune retires identity-less rows as permanently unactionable, on the premise that no relink can ever resolve them. That premise is false: realign has had a name-similarity tier all along, unreachable from prune only because it lived in another package. This moves the ladder into `internal/identity` and makes realign its first caller. Prune joins in the next PR.
- **`identity.ResolveHeuristic`** owns the confidence floor, the margin rule (#672) and the untagged-positional degradation. Realign's two inline helpers (`heuristicNameGuard`, `bestRivalScore`) are **deleted**, not left beside it -- the issue asks for reuse, and a second matcher kept in place is exactly what that warning is about.
- **Reviewers look here first:** `Candidate` gains a `Stem` field distinct from `Ref`, and the resolver takes **two** candidate slices rather than one. Both are load-bearing; rationale below.

## Linked issue

Part of #740

Deliberately `Part of`, not `Closes` -- this lands the shared resolver only. The prune reorder that actually fixes the data loss, and the recovery pass for rows already retired, follow as separate PRs.

## Design notes

**Targets and rivals are separate sets.** Targets are what an orphan may attach TO; rivals are everything the name must distinguish it FROM. Realign's only legal destination is the lone sidecar-less gap, but its rival set is every audio file in the directory **including ones that already have sidecars**: an orphan matching the already-paired track next door just as well as it matches the gap carries a name signal that cannot tell the tracks apart. Collapsing the two sets reinstates #672 -- mutation-verified, the near-tie resolves `Unique` instead of `Conflict`. Prune will pass one slice for both; realign passes different ones.

**`Ref` vs `Stem`.** `Ref` is an opaque handle the caller round-trips back out of a `Unique` verdict -- a full path for realign, a row handle for prune. `Stem` is filename-derived name evidence. Keeping them one field meant scoring a full path against a bare stem, which depressed every similarity score (see below). Prune constructs `Candidate` with keyed literals, so it is unaffected by the new field.

## Why the safety argument is realign's suite, not my tests

**Realign's existing suite caught two real bugs in my first cut**, neither visible from the new tests (which passed the same slice twice and used bare stems as refs):

1. **`Ref` was scored as name evidence.** A genuine production pairing fell to 0.45 and was skipped -- the test asserting it is explicitly labelled a real production pairing that must not regress.
2. **The positional degradation was too strict.** Keyed on "one target AND no rivals", it broke realign pairing a lone untagged orphan with the lone gap when other audio sat in the directory. An instrumental `.txt` with no name evidence on either side must still re-attach. Now keyed on target count alone: a second TARGET is a guess, a rival is not.

That is the argument for this PR: a promotion that preserves behavior, proven by tests written before the refactor existed.

## Pre-flight checklist

- [x] Pre-push gate green locally: all twelve steps, zero test failures.
- [x] Code review pass complete; three genuine lint findings fixed before pushing (two `revive` doc-comment placements caused by inserting the result struct between the doc comment and its function; one `gosec` G602 slice-index, eliminated by tracking the winning `Ref` directly rather than suppressed with a `//nolint`).
- [x] Single commit.
- [x] Label set on `gh pr create --label ...`.
- [x] UAT: N/A -- no user-visible behavior change; realign's resolver reaches the same verdicts, asserted by its own suite.
- [x] Screenshot: N/A -- no web-UI change.
- [x] `make ui`: N/A -- no `.templ` or CSS change.
- [x] Migration: N/A -- no schema change.

## Test plan

- [x] `make gate` passes: conflict markers, gofmt, `make ui`, build, `go test -race` + coverage, patch coverage, coverage-floor ratchet, codecov validation, golangci-lint, actionlint, ci-shards, govulncheck.
- [x] Patch coverage **100.00% (62/62 executable lines)**.
- [x] **New tests confirmed to fail against unfixed code.** `ResolveHeuristic` was stubbed to return zero values first; four subtests failed at their assertions with real printed values before the implementation existed.
- [x] **All four decision paths mutation-tested**, each failing at its own assertion rather than at the build:
  - drop the margin rule -> the near-tie resolves `Unique` (the #672 defect)
  - drop the confidence floor -> a dissimilar pair resolves `Unique`
  - make untagged-lone a conflict -> positional degradation breaks
  - let untagged-many resolve -> a guess is accepted
  - collapse targets into rivals -> the sidecar-bearing rival stops blocking
- [x] `internal/realign` suite passes **unchanged** -- the load-bearing check for a promotion.
- [x] **Surface stated explicitly.** `internal/identity` (new resolver) and `internal/realign` (wired to it, duplicates deleted). `internal/prune` is untouched in this PR and its tests pass; it changes in the next one.
- [ ] Reviewer follow-ups:
  - [ ] The N:M matcher (`resolveNameMatch`) stays private in realign, per the issue's own scoping. It shares the primitives but not this resolver, so the two tiers are only partly unified -- worth confirming you are happy with that boundary before PR 2 builds on it.
  - [ ] `HeuristicResult.RunnerUp` is meaningful only when `HasRival`. A caller reading `RunnerUp` without checking `HasRival` would see a plain `0`, which is indistinguishable from a genuinely zero-scoring rival. Documented on the struct; tell me if you would rather it were a pointer.

author: gemisis
body:
The ordering and chunking half of the design agreed on #474. Breakpoint eligibility is
deliberately untouched — that is the half that regressed twice and it wants the reporter's
request dumps before anyone changes it again.

## Why the ordering was wrong

A provider caches the prompt by **prefix**: it stores everything up to a marker and reuses
that only if every byte in front of the marker is identical. So one region that changes
invalidates the cache for every region behind it, and the ordering of the prompt is worth
money.

That ordering was inferred from each region's **kind**, and the inference is wrong in the
direction that costs the most:

- A `pinned` region sounds immutable and is written constantly — `context_write` into a
  findings region is an ordinary agent move, and tool routing sends read results straight
  into one.
- A `compact_history` region sounds settled and gains an entry every time compaction fires.

Both were sorted to the front, where their churn invalidated everything behind them.

## What replaces it

```toml
task    = { kind = "pinned",  volatility = "stable" }
sources = { kind = "pinned",  volatility = "grows" }
scratch = { kind = "hashmap", volatility = "rewritten" }
```

| value | sorted | also |
|---|---|---|
| `stable` | first | forms the prefix everything else caches behind |
| `grows` | next | **split into chunks**, so its settled part caches while only the newest is re-sent |
| `rewritten` | last | invalidates nothing but itself |

`grows` needs both mechanisms: ordering alone does not help a growing region, because
rendered as one block it offers exactly one boundary and that boundary moves every time it
grows.

## Measured live

Same binary, same agent, 24 iterations either way. The only difference is whether the
manifest declares:

| manifest | prompt | cached | cache writes | hit rate | cost/iter |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| undeclared | 173,957 | **0** | 115,635 | **0.0%** | 13,271 |
| declared | 41,813 | **199,937** | 58,716 | **66.5%** | **5,633** |

**58% cheaper per iteration.** Both arms ran the same number of turns, so this is not the
run-length confound that made an earlier comparison in this thread misleading — that one
compared runs of 18 and 26 turns and I read the raw totals before normalising.

## Three things that keep it honest

**The default is `rewritten`**, the pessimistic value. An unclassified region is assumed to
move and sorted late, so an un-annotated blueprint is never made *worse* by this, and
annotating is a strict improvement. An optimistic default is precisely how inferring from the
kind went wrong.

**A misspelled value is refused at load** rather than falling back to the default, because
the default is the worst placement — a typo would quietly cost the author exactly the caching
they were asking for.

**The declaration is checked, not trusted.** A wrong `stable` is worse than no declaration:
it puts churn at the front of the prefix, the most destructive position there is, and puts it
there *because* we believed the label. The blocks are hashed every request anyway, so a
region that declares itself stable and keeps changing is named in the log with what to write
instead.

## Also

A breakpoint is no longer spent on a prefix too short for the provider to store. Anthropic
caches nothing below ~1,024 tokens, and a dumped request showed one of the four sitting on a
**269-byte block**, where it could never be read back.

Several existing tests used one-token fixture blocks and so lost their breakpoints under that
rule — correctly. Their fixtures are now realistically sized, so they test what they meant to
test (how runs are grouped) rather than the new size rule.

## Checks

Full suite green, clippy clean under `-D warnings`, all four coverage gates at 100%, docs
updated with a "what caching costs" section for blueprint authors.

body:
## Summary
This PR migrates the `ApiKeyFilter` and `ConcurrencyLimitFilter` from Micronaut's `@Filter`/`HttpServerFilter` pattern (which runs on the Netty event loop by default) to `@RequestFilter` methods wired to `TaskExecutors.BLOCKING`. This ensures that blocking I/O operations—particularly the rate limiter's synchronous Redis calls—never starve the event loop, keeping the liveness probe responsive even under degraded conditions. Additionally, it hardens API key authentication with SHA-256 hashing and adds comprehensive test coverage.

## Key Changes

**Filter Migration (BUDG-03/BUDG-04)**
- Converted `ApiKeyFilter` from `@Filter`/`HttpServerFilter` to `@RequestFilter` with `@ExecuteOn(TaskExecutors.BLOCKING)`
- Converted `ConcurrencyLimitFilter` from `@Filter`/`HttpServerFilter` to `@RequestFilter` with `@ExecuteOn(TaskExecutors.BLOCKING)`
- Both filters now execute off the Netty event loop, preventing event loop starvation when Redis is latent
- Added `@Order` annotations to maintain filter execution sequence (auth before rate limiting)

**Security Hardening (SEC-04)**
- `ApiKeyFilter` now compares API keys using SHA-256 digests via `MessageDigest.isEqual()` instead of plaintext string comparison
- Configuration accepts both raw dev keys and pre-hashed `sha256:<hex>` entries; both resolve to the same digest at boot
- Timing-safe comparison prevents length-based information leakage on failed authentication attempts
- `ProductionSecurityGuard` validates that production configurations use only hashed keys

**Logging Configuration (SEC-06)**
- Updated `logback.xml` to default app logger to INFO level in all environments
- Added support for `LOG_LEVEL_APP` environment variable override without requiring a rebuild
- Added unit test (`LogbackLevelUnitTest`) to verify the override mechanism works correctly

**Avro Schema Governance (SEC-01)**
- Added `payments.avro.auto-register` configuration property (defaults to false in production)
- `ProductionSecurityGuard` now validates that auto-registration is disabled in production
- Ensures schema governance remains the registry's responsibility, never inferred from producer payloads

## Test Coverage

**New Integration Tests**
- `LivenessUnderRedisLatencyIT`: Verifies liveness probe responds in <500ms even with 2s Redis latency and concurrent admission requests in flight
- `ConcurrencyLimitFilterOffEventLoopIT`: Proves the rate limiter's Redis calls execute on virtual threads (off the event loop) using `ThreadCapturingRedisCommandsProvider`

**New Unit Tests**
- `ApiKeyFilterUnitTest`: Validates 401/pass-through semantics, plaintext/hashed key matching, and `@ExecuteOn(TaskExecutors.BLOCKING)` annotation presence
- `ConcurrencyLimitFilterUnitTest`: Validates admit/reject behavior and `@ExecuteOn(TaskExecutors.BLOCKING)` annotation presence
- `LogbackLevelUnitTest`: Validates logback configuration defaults and environment variable override
- `ProductionSecurityGuardUnitTest`: Updated to test hashed key format and Avro auto-register validation

**Test Infrastructure**
- `SlowRedisProxy`: Local TCP proxy that injects configurable response latency to simulate degraded Redis without additional Testcontainers dependencies
- `ThreadCapturingRedisCommandsProvider`: Test-only Redis provider that records whether calls execute on virtual threads

## Implementation Details

- Filter methods return `null` to proceed or a `MutableHttpResponse<?>` to short-circuit the chain, replacing the reactive `Publisher` pattern
- API key hashing happens at boot time; request-time comparison is O(n) over configured keys but constant-time per key via `MessageDigest.isEqual()`
- The liveness probe in `LivenessUnderRedisLatencyIT` uses the JDK `HttpClient` rather than Micronaut's Netty-based client to avoid confounding server-side results with client-side connection pool behavior

body:
PR #6 was closed unmerged, so this reopens that work rebuilt on current `main` — plus the browser coverage `main`'s README says the Roku is missing, and a real bug that writing the coverage turned up.

## The television is simulated now, not just drawn

The Roku is a box on **HDMI 1**. The set it is plugged into has HDMI 2 (a disc player), HDMI 3 and AV (nothing plugged in), and an antenna input that was never tuned. "Check which input the TV is on" is the first question on a large share of real support calls, and it could not be practised while the television was only a picture frame.

The set draws **its own on-screen display** — square corners, flat grey, no purple anywhere — because telling the box's screens from the set's is the entire skill.

Switch away from HDMI 1 and the box keeps running behind it: everything works, and the customer sees *No Signal*. The remote goes deaf, because nothing it sends can be seen. Three ways back, each gated on a setting that already existed:

| Route | Works when |
|---|---|
| **Input** on the remote | the remote has been through *Settings › Remotes & devices › Set up remote for TV control* |
| **Home** | HDMI-CEC one-touch play is on under *Settings › System › Control other devices (CEC)* |
| **Input** on the set itself | always — the fallback when the remote is the problem |

## Roku's real button chords

| Chord | What it does |
|---|---|
| Home ×5, Up, Rewind ×2, Fast forward ×2 | reboots the device |
| Home ×5, Fast forward ×3, Rewind ×2 | the platform secret screen |
| Home ×5, Right, Left, Right, Left, Right | jumps to the network menu |

The secret screen is plain and monospaced on purpose, and every figure on it is read off the simulated device.

## The catalogue is jokes now

Every title is a **show-within-a-show** — the sort that only exists inside somebody else's sitcom. The developer names on channel pages are the fictional companies that made them, the neighbours' Wi-Fi networks are the names people really give their routers, and the search suggestions, live guide and voice results are in on it. None of it changes behaviour; every support flow is still straight.

## A bug the coverage found

The player owns a one-second interval and only cleared it on the **Back** path. Pressing **Home** goes through the shell, which replaces the stack from underneath the screen — so the clock kept ticking on detached DOM for the life of the page, and the resume point was never banked. Leave a film by Home and it did not come back in Continue Watching.

Fixed with a lifecycle hook rather than a special case: `renderTop` tears the outgoing screen down before its DOM goes, and the player disposes there as well as on exit. Any screen that owns a timer now has somewhere to stop it.

Worth noting: **my first version of the assertion did not catch this.** It checked whether the player's DOM was gone, which `goHome()` does anyway. It now asserts the consequence a viewer would notice — that the resume point survives leaving by either route. Reverting the fix fails the suite on Home and passes on Back, which is exactly the shape of the bug.

## Roku coverage in `tools/smoke.mjs`

`main`'s README said the Roku had only the parse and reference gates. It now has the browser gate too:

- walks the **entire settings tree**, calling every `value()` and `detail()` closure — they are evaluated lazily against live state, so this is the easiest place in the project to hide a reference error — then renders every screen that has rows
- opens **every channel page** and every screen, asserting each has something the remote can reach
- checks **no screen repeats a focus id**, since Back restores by that id
- switches the television through **all five inputs**, and asserts one-touch play works with HDMI-CEC on and stays quiet with it off
- leaves the player by **each exit** to prove the clock stops and the resume point survives

Both READMEs are updated to match.

## Testing

All three gates pass from a clean checkout:

```
python3 tools/check-syntax.py   → All syntax checks passed
python3 tools/check-refs.py     → All reference checks passed
node tools/smoke.mjs            → mac 31 apps · iphone 51 apps ·
                                  roku 13 screens, 43 channels, 48 titles, 5 inputs
```

Plus the visual suites: the full screen tour, the input/CEC/chord suite, and the site index with all four project pages loading — no console or page errors in any run.

body:
Closes #2.

Both fixes are the same shape: a result that could be read as a finding when it was really an absence. Each carries a spec that **fails against 0.2.0** and passes here.

### `#total` is nil, not 0, for a record that does not exist

`0` is a legitimate total — `v=spf1 -all` costs exactly that — so using it for "no record" let a caller that skipped `#published?` report *"this record costs 0 lookups"* about a domain with none. `#headroom` follows: it cannot say how much room is left in a record that does not exist. A record that legitimately costs nothing still reports `0`, and there is a spec pinning that distinction.

### Apex duplicates are reported separately from chain duplicates

RFC 7208 §4.5 — *"A domain… MUST NOT publish more than one version 1 SPF record"* — makes a second record a permerror at the apex and in the chain alike. But the apex is not *in* the chain; it is the record being priced.

Folding them together meant the same domain audited two ways disagreed: with `record:` supplied the apex was never added, resolving it ourselves it was. A caller that raises its own duplicate-record defect from the records **it** resolved would have raised it twice the moment it stopped passing `record:`, with nothing to warn it.

`#apex_duplicated?` answers `true`/`false` when we resolved the apex, and `nil` — *cannot say* — when the record was handed to us or DNS did not answer. `#duplicated_in_chain` no longer contains the audited hostname.

### Breaking, deliberately

`#duplicated_in_chain` dropping the apex is a behaviour change on a public method. 0.2.0 has a single known consumer, which takes the safe path through both bugs and needs no change.

Live-set RPE was also a 6–10 dropdown, and tapping it on a saved set did nothing until you hit the check to edit. ## Extra exercises - Extra exercises (added or created during the live workout) show a **REMOVE** control for that session. - If you **complete a working set** on the extra and finish the workout, it is saved onto that day’s catalog for next time. - If you **remove** it during the session (or discard / finish without training it), it is dropped from the catalog and will not appear on future sessions unless you add it again. - Other-day catalog rows are not deleted — only this session’s extra is dropped; a trained other-day extra is cloned onto this day at finish. ## RPE - Scale is **1–10**, shown as a compact 5×2 pill grid (not a 10-item list). - Tapping a pill on a saved set unlocks that row the same way weight/reps do, and writes RPE immediately — no need to tap the check first. - Tap the selected value again to clear. ## Notes No SQL migration. New live-session creates start `active: false` until a working set is finished, so a discarded extra cannot leak into the next workout. RPE was already 1–10 in the database (`session_logs_rpe_range`).

`.claude/skills/frontend-design/SKILL.md` is written for greenfield work: pick a

## Summary

Fix for Attendance Print V2: the Trainer/Assessor verification block (and footer) were being forced wholesale to page 2, leaving a large blank gap on page 1.

body:
## Summary

`SectorAccessPolicy::from_schema` read `x-disclosure` from the **root** `properties` map only. `filter_by_audience` classifies keys at **every** nesting depth. So a property annotated `"x-disclosure": "restricted"` inside an object, an array's `items`, or a `definitions` block was not in the policy map at all, fell through to `default_disclosure` — `Public` — and was served to anyone.

The author had done everything right. The annotation sat exactly where the constructor's own doc comment says to put it, and it did nothing. Neither build-time gate looked deep enough to notice.

Found during a full audit.

## Nothing leaked — and that is the reason to fix it now

Every nested property in the tree today sits under a public parent and was correctly public anyway. I verified this exhaustively: a differential check across all 28 embedded schemas × all 3 audiences finds the served field set **identical** before and after.

The defect was never a live leak. It was that annotating a nested field correctly *would not have helped* — and battery went from 16 to 44 nested properties in one schema version.

## Changes

- **`from_schema` collects from every depth** — nested `properties`, `items`, `additionalProperties`, `definitions`/`$defs`, and `allOf`/`anyOf`/`oneOf`. `$ref` is deliberately not followed (definitions are walked directly; leaf-name matching makes that equivalent, and it means a cyclic `$ref` cannot loop the walk).
- **`disclosure_for_field` is deterministic.** It matched after normalisation but returned the first hit from `HashMap` iteration — unspecified, reseeded per map — so `jwsSignature` against a map also holding `jws_signature` could answer `Conformity` once and `Public` the next call, in one process. It now considers every match and keeps the most restrictive. Pinned by a 512-iteration test that rebuilds the map each time (a reused map would report stable and prove nothing).
- **184 nested properties annotated** across 19 schema files, each with the class the filter already applied.
- **Both gates walk the constructor's tree**, and a third rejects one name declared in two classes.

## The constraint that shaped this, and what is deliberately left

A nested class can only be more restrictive than `public` where the leaf name is **globally unambiguous**, because matching is path-insensitive. Two things bound it:

1. **Within a schema** — `name` and `casNumber` are shared between a restricted `materialComposition` and a public `criticalRawMaterials`.
2. **Across the document** — a sector policy is applied to the *whole passport*. A schema restricting `countryOfOrigin` would redact `materials[].countryOfOrigin` from the envelope, which is Annex III public content.

The second was caught by the committed AAS environment fixtures, which failed with `countryOfOrigin` vanishing from the public electronics projection. Over-redaction is not the safe direction here — it makes the public passport omit content the regulation requires.

Where a name is shared, the **enclosing object** carries the restriction and the filter removes the whole subtree before reaching the leaf. Expressing it on the leaf needs a **path-aware matcher**; that is a larger change and is not in this PR. The limit is now documented on `SectorAccessPolicy` and enforced by a gate instead of being rediscovered.

## Verification

- Differential check: 84 (schema × audience) combinations, **0 behaviour differences**.
- Negative control — remove one nested annotation and the gate names it precisely:
  ```
  battery v2.6.0: these properties declare no usable x-disclosure class, so they would
  default to public: [("hazardousSubstances[].casNumber", "<missing>")]
  ```
- The widened gate immediately found 8 properties under `stateOfHealth`'s `oneOf` branches that my first pass missed — the gate is stricter than the tooling that produced the annotations, which is the right way round.
- Committed AAS environment fixtures unchanged.
- `just check` green.

## Checklist

- [x] Tests added or updated for new behaviour
- [x] `just lint` passes locally
- [x] `just fmt` applied
- [x] `just test` passes
- [x] No secrets, credentials, or `.env` files in the diff
- [x] Documentation updated if public API changed — `Disclosure::most_restrictive` added; CHANGELOG updated

body:
## The bug
In general (non-RAG) mode you can attach an image, it renders in the bubble — and the model answers without ever seeing it.

## Root cause (two layers)
1. The general-mode branch sends only `system + history` to the LLM; `attachments` was **never consulted** (RAG mode has a dedicated attachment path; general mode had none).
2. Even with that fixed, raw image bytes were only retained when **CLIP visual search** is configured (default-off) — so on standard deployments the pixels were already gone.

## Fix
- **Any model:** the attachment's extracted text (incl. vision-OCR done at upload time) is injected as system context — parity with how RAG mode treats attachments.
- **Vision models:** raw image bytes (capped at 4, same bound as the RAG vision path) attach to your latest message and the answer generates via `generate_vision`. Trade-off carried over from the existing vision path: no streaming variant exists, so image answers arrive as one chunk instead of token-by-token.
- **Retention:** image bytes now kept for every `image/*` upload — safe because SessionAttachment is per-request, in-memory, never serialized.

## Verification
5 new unit tests on the extracted helpers (context injection, empty-extraction skip, 4-image cap, non-image no-op). fmt clean, workspace clippy `-D warnings` clean, 227 lib tests green.

## Live test after deploy
General mode → attach a photo → "what's in this image?" → the answer should describe it. Expect the answer in one chunk (buffered vision), not a token stream.

author: nateisern
body:
Refs #434 — the **layout half only**. `ar.json` for these two apps (1,061 strings
under the `validate:i18n-strings` parity gate) is the other half and is
deliberately not in this PR, so #434 stays open.

## The class migration is four edits, and that was measured

The census did not use hand-written patterns: it lifted the six rule regexes
**verbatim** out of `scripts/validate-rtl-logical-classes.mjs` (asserted
byte-identical) and ran them over both packages with an empty exception list.

```
dashboard/components/shell/Sidebar.tsx      ml-auto -> ms-auto
pos/components/shell/Sidebar.tsx            ml-auto -> ms-auto
pos/components/register/CatalogPane.tsx     pr-4    -> pe-4
pos/components/register/ProductTile.tsx     left-2  -> start-2
```

It is that small because both apps lay out with `gap-` on flex containers rather
than directional spacing, and `flex-direction` mirrors itself.

**The sizing held, and then the tree moved.** #367 landed while this was in
flight and added a `text-right` to the wizard review panel — the widened gate
caught it, which is the gate doing its job on its first day. So the final shape
is 4 conversions and **2** exception entries, not 1.

## Two findings stay PHYSICAL

Both get a reasoned `KNOWN_EXCEPTIONS` entry with an **exact count** (#448):

| file | pattern | count |
|---|---|---|
| `pos/app/(app)/index.tsx` | `border-l` | 1 |
| `dashboard/components/catalog-authoring/ReviewPanel.tsx` | `text-right` | 2 |

`border-s-*` emits `borderInlineStartWidth`, which RN 0.85.3 does not register;
`text-start` is rejected outright by react-native-css's `parseTextAlign`. Both
compile clean and fail only on a device. The `text-right` count is 2 for ONE
decision — the class, plus the comment above it that documents the choice, since
this guard matches on text and does not strip comments.

## Where the bootstrap lives, and why

In `@mercaria/ui/src/i18n/`, via the `onLocaleApplied` hook
`create-i18n-store.ts`'s own docblock reserved for "the change that has a caller
for it". This change has two callers.

Per-app was the alternative and it is structurally worse: the store owns
rehydration and deliberately does not export its handle, so an app cannot reach
that moment without a `useEffect` — and direction must settle *before* render
(`I18nManager.isRTL` is external mutable state). It would also have made three
copies of "which languages are RTL".

The mechanism is **split in two, and the split is load-bearing**:

- `rtl-locales.ts` — the DECISION. Imports nothing at all.
- `layout-direction.ts` — the APPLICATION. Needs `I18nManager`.

`react-native` cannot be imported outside a bundler, and none of these four
packages has a test runner, so keeping the decision pure is the only thing that
lets a guard exercise the real function instead of a copy of its logic.

This agrees with #437 from the other side: its merge is the **intersection** of
shared copy with what each app ships, so an app can neither gain a locale it
cannot mirror nor mirror one it does not ship.

## An RTL language with no bundle stays LTR — checked, not assumed

`enableFallback` renders English, so mirroring a locale nobody shipped copy for
produces an English screen laid out right-to-left: wrong in a way neither half
explains on its own. `scripts/validate-rtl-direction.mjs` asserts it, written as
a **biconditional** (mirror exactly when the language is RTL *and* a bundle
exists) so it survives `ar.json` arriving rather than failing that PR.

It runs inside `validate:rtl-classes`, so CI gains no step and the guard list is
unchanged in number.

## The widened scope

`SCANNED_PREFIXES` covers all four client packages, in the **same** change that
migrated them. The vacuity floor is re-derived from the tree — **390**, above the
388 that would survive losing the smallest prefix. It was 360 against a 422-file
tree earlier in this same PR; #367 and #437 landed 30 files in between and 360
silently stopped covering `packages/pos/`. A floor is a measurement, and it goes
stale in the green direction.

## Verification

All seven `validate:*` guards, `lint`, and all five typechecks exit 0 (real exit
codes, not piped).

Mutation-tested, each **proven applied by diff first**, each caught **by name**,
each restored:

- physical class reintroduced in the **dashboard** → red naming the file
- physical class reintroduced in the **POS** → red naming the file
- a second excused-shape utility riding into **each** excused file → red naming
  "the count went UP"
- direction guard: bundle check removed → red; always-false → red; parser broken
  → red

One of those mutations **found a real hole in my own guard**: commenting a subtag
out left the quoted string in range, so the drift check reported clean over a
real divergence. It now strips comments before parsing. That is in the diff.

**No device was run.** Whether the mirrored layout is *correct* is a rendering
property, and nothing here or in CI renders a screen. This PR asserts the
utilities are logical and the direction rule is right; it cannot assert the
result looks right in Arabic.

## Residual, stated rather than worked around

- **`pos/components/register/VariantPickerSheet.tsx:30` uses
  `<SheetContent side="right">`** — the `panel`/`sheet` blocker #428 hit and
  left. The physical `side` prop plus `translateX` is an API change plus an
  animation change, not a class swap. **The POS variant picker will not mirror
  until #429.**
- The storefront keeps its own copy of the RTL rule, because collapsing it means
  moving its hand-built `I18n` and hand-rolled store — that is #435, and doing it
  here would couple a layout change to the storefront's locale plumbing for no
  behaviour gain. Until then the two sets are **compared on every run**, so they
  cannot drift silently.
- No restart notice in either app. `directionRestartRequired` is the storefront's
  shape; it cannot fire in these two while neither ships an RTL bundle, and the
  POS has no language picker to render one on. It belongs with the bundles.

Refs #434. Residual: #429, #435.

author: monglong0214
body:
Stacked on #717 (the temp-filename fix). Partially addresses #716; the observation is #714.

The Windows run reported `cursor` as:

```
config is not parseable JSON: Unexpected end of JSON input
```

That message says a parse of an empty string happened. It does not say **which file** was parsed — and the counter-check on that machine found valid, byte-identical JSON.

Both can be true. This command reads `%USERPROFILE%\.cursor\mcp.json` and only that, while Cursor keeps configuration in more than one place. The installer and the person checking it can each be right about a different file, and nothing in the output separates them. That is why #716 records the cursor *outcome* as confirmed and its *reason* as not.

**Waiting for that machine's transcript would not have settled it.** The path was never recorded anywhere, so no transcript could contain it. A receipt that names the failure but not its subject sends the next reader to a file that is fine.

## Change

All seven read/write failure paths across the JSON and TOML hosts now lead with the path:

| before | after |
|---|---|
| `config is not parseable JSON: …` | `<path> is not parseable JSON: …` |
| `mcpServers is not an object` | `mcpServers in <path> is not an object` |
| `atomic config write failed: …` | `<path> could not be written atomically: …` |
| `could not read config: …` | `<path> could not be read: …` |
| `commitlore registration has no runnable command and args` | `the commitlore registration in <path> has no runnable…` |

No schema change: `commitlore_installer_hosts.v1` keeps its fields, and `detail` was already the free-text field a human reads.

## Why now

A Windows agent is about to re-run this on the machine that produced #714. Without this, that run produces the same undecidable output and the cursor question stays open for another round trip.

## Verification

Reverting the three message changes fails all 3 new cases. The tests assert the **path**, not the wording, and drive the real enumeration with an empty `PATH` and a scratch home so detection turns on the fixture rather than on whatever the developer has installed.

10 cases pass across the three `installer-hosts` suites; `tsc --noEmit` clean; `build:canonical` then `artifact:verify` → `310a0d2420e1bf4196581913d0fc1752ea8eee25510741c683d61d67897510e6`.

This makes the cursor question **answerable** on the next Windows run. It does not answer it, and it does not touch cause 2 (`hasCommand` / `PATHEXT` / `shell: false`), which still needs that machine.

body:
Framework half of #303, rebased on the #305 merge. Ryan's ruling applied: a pending client-handled call surfaces as `input_required` — no silent default timeout.

## Changes
1. **`sessionId` on `ClientToolCall` and handler `ToolCtx`** — the handle closed over it and withheld it; foreground-ness was unanswerable without it.
2. **`client.session(id)` memoized** (in `makeSessionHandle`, so the client/app/gateway doors are all one door) — subscription and pending fold are singletons per session. Beyond the AC: `destroySession` verbs release the handle; eviction on `close()` alone left a memoized handle subscribed to a session the server had forgotten.
3. **`use(tools, { ctx })` per-dispatch contributor**, typed via the previously-dormant `ToolCtxExtensions` augmentation seam; spread before framework fields so contributed keys can't shadow the call identity. Foreground stays an adopter concern: `ctx.sessionId === active()`.
4. **`tool:command:client-call`** — the `requiresResponse` relay wrapped in an operation so the suspension has both edges on the bus (`request()` publishes only the ask; the answer rides the inbox). Its requested/terminal pair folds into the SAME blocked Set as `elicitation:command:elicit`: ADR 101 invariants hold verbatim (status-guarded, end-beats-blocked, balanced on every exit, concurrent asks of either kind are one state). Hooks derive `onBefore/onAfterToolClientCall` for free.
5. **README truth** — the timeout-fallback claim removed from all three places it appeared; docs now state: no default timeout, an unanswered call holds the execution and reads `input_required`, `responseTimeoutMs` + `defaultResult` is the opt-in.

## Tests
New: two-sessions-one-client e2e (background session's call dispatched with its own sessionId while the status channel reads `idle → running → input_required → running → idle`), handle memoization + destroy-door release, ctx contributor evaluated per dispatch and unable to shadow framework fields. Positive controls verified both directions.
Touched packages 1167 passed / 0 failed pre-rebase; post-rebase 956/956 across session, tool-executor, transport-in-process, client-core; session tsc clean on the merged harness.

Downstream next: knowify Slice B (tool-routing registry per open session) + retiring the `hasOpenTurn` fallback term, both on the next version cut.

body:
## WHAT

Two internal-only tidy-ups from the pre-1.0 refactoring audit (#781), touching no behaviour and no
public signature:

- `SpannerChangeStreamSourceConfig` carried fourteen package-private fields *and* a full set of
  fourteen public getters, and `SpannerChangeStreamSource` — the only class that could — read six of
  those fields directly at eight sites, including re-doing inline the `Optional.ofNullable(...)`
  that `getResumeFallback()` already does. The fields are now `private`, and the source reads through
  the getters. Its two siblings, `SpannerSourceConfig` and `SpannerSinkConfig`, were already
  private-field-plus-getter, so this leaves one idiom in the module rather than two.
- Thirteen inline fully-qualified names across eight files are replaced by imports: `java.util.UUID` in
  `RowDataToSpannerValueConverter` and `StructToRowDataConverter`, `java.util.LinkedHashSet` three
  times in `SpannerTableReadResolver`, `java.io.IOException` in a `SpannerBatchReadSource` method
  signature, `java.time.Instant` in `SpannerChangeStreamStatements` and
  `SpannerChangeStreamGoogleSqlRecordDecoder`, and `java.util.Optional` in the two change-stream
  source files above.

## WHY

Two ways to reach the same state is one more than a reader has to check, and the direction that
was being used was the one that bypasses the class's own null handling — the `Optional` wrapper on
`resumeFallback` existed and was re-implemented at the call site. Making the fields private removes
the choice rather than documenting it.

None of the thirteen fully-qualified names was forced: it was verified that no file among them imports
a conflicting simple name, and every other file in the module imports these types normally. They
are the kind of thing spotless does not touch and a reader stumbles over.

Implements Wave 1 item 3 of CI-PERFORMANCE-PLAN for this repo. The other four repos already did this (printer #99, deploy #111, sofra #150, frontend #502).

## Why

"Dependabot PRs are paused" is a **standing decision** in the workspace CLAUDE.md — but the bot was still being paid to open them. Measured on this repo: **21 Dependabot / `dependabot/*`-branch workflow runs** in the last 200 runs, and **7 PRs open since 2026-07-13** (#333, #235, #233, #178, #177, #175, #174), all sitting unmerged and rebasing.

This makes the status quo **honest** rather than changing it.

## What

`open-pull-requests-limit: 0` on both update blocks — the documented way to switch off *version-update* PRs while leaving Dependabot **security updates fully on**. That is why the file stays instead of being deleted.

Version drift is the accepted cost, and it was already being accepted — the PRs were not being merged. **No CVE gate changes**: OSV-Scanner, Trivy, nuget audit and SonarCloud still run on every PR, and `security-audit.yml` still runs weekly. Re-enable by restoring the limits.

author: layott
body:
Fans pick a squad of real players from a real AFC event before it starts and score from what those players actually do. Spec: `WEBSITE/tasks/fantasy-league-spec.md`, approved by the owner.

**Adds no organizer work.** Every score is computed from match stats that were being entered anyway.

## The constraint that shaped it

The only per-player figures AFC reliably records are **kills and sometimes MVP**. Damage, assists and deaths have columns and are mostly empty. So scoring uses kills, MVP, team placement and whether the player was fielded, and nothing else. Scoring on a column nobody fills would make a fan's total depend on whether an organizer had a spare five minutes. The damage rule ships at 0 points and waits for the data.

## Pricing is ranked, not proportional

Measured before building it: across the 254 players with 5+ maps, the best gets **4.8x** the kills-per-map of the median. Price proportionally off a 100-seed pot and the best player costs 96 seeds, so nobody can ever pick him and the budget has done the opposite of its job.

So players are spread evenly across an **8 to 32 seed band by where they rank**. Verified on event 130 (343 players):

| Squad | Cost | Possible? |
|---|---|---|
| The five best | 183 | No, correctly |
| Five median players | exactly 100 | Yes |

**The team carries a premium too**, because a player on a strong team scores twice. Ranked on the team's actual placement record, **not** the tier field: 129 of 130 ranked teams are Tier 3 and `Team.team_tier` is `"3"` for all 620, so a tier premium would bonus one team and nobody else. Average finish spans 2.56 to 10.00 across 69 teams, which separates them properly.

## Scores are never stored as truth

`FantasyPoints` is a cache that **replaces** rather than accumulates, because AFC corrects results and a correction that lowers a score has to work as well as one that raises it.

## Squad rules return reasons, not a boolean

Every rule reports pass or fail with the fan's own position against it, and they are re-checked server-side on save, because a squad that breaks the budget does not look wrong, it wins.

## Verified

End to end on live data: 101 players priced, legal squad at 49 of 100 seeds, 20 score rows across 20 matches, standings computed, idempotent on re-run. Every admin endpoint exercised including both refusals (opening without prices → 400, editing a frozen rule → 409). 26 tests.

author: emilhvitfeldt
body:
Works through the "Edge cases every parser must cover" section of `CONTRIBUTING.md` for `lda`, `qda`, `fda`, `sda`, `sparsediscrim`, `mixOmics`, `ksvm`, `LiblineaR`, `klaR::NaiveBayes`, `naivebayes::naive_bayes` and `nullmodel`. Tests only, no `R/` or `NEWS.md` changes.

Threshold precision does not apply to any of these models: none of them stores a split threshold, so there is no comparison whose precision could decide anything.

## Coverage added

- **Factors and categorical splits.** A level containing `:`, an unused level, an ordered predictor, and a level colliding with another variable's name, for every model that accepts factors. `LiblineaR` and `sda` (matrix interface) take a numeric matrix only, so factors reach them through parsnip if at all.
- **Missing values.** `NA` in the newdata and `NA` in the training data, compared against `predict()` on the rows the reference keeps. `predict.fda()` and `predict.ksvm()` drop incomplete rows rather than returning `NA`, which the tests account for explicitly.
- **Options the parser might ignore.** `LiblineaR` `bias = 5`, `cost` and `wi`; `ksvm` `C`, `epsilon` and `class.weights`. Existing tests already covered `prior`, `method`, `nu`, `subset`, `lambda`, `laplace`, `diagonal` and `scale`.
- **Degenerate fit shapes.** Single-column model matrices, a collinear (`NA` coefficient) `lda` fit, single-row `nullmodel` training data, an unused outcome level, and an `NA` in the training outcome.

## Defects found

Each is recorded as a skipped test carrying its reproducer, not as a failing assertion.

1. **`lda` and `qda` wrongly reject a factor level containing `:`.** `acceptable_contrasts()` splits the model matrix column names on `:` before matching them against the levels, so a level named `c:d` is read as the level `c` of an unknown variable and the fit is rejected as a non-treatment contrast. Bypassing the check makes the parse agree with `predict()` to 2e-16, and `mda::fda()`, which has no such check, handles the same data correctly.
2. **`ksvm` is silently wrong for a factor level that is not a syntactic name.** `ksvm()` runs its column names through `make.names()`, so a level `c:d` becomes the column `fc.d`. The parser reads the level back off that name and emits `f == "c.d"`, which matches no row. Max abs diff 0.90 for a regression fit, 0.75 for classification probabilities; a level containing a space is wrong the same way.
3. **`sparsediscrim` is silently wrong for a coefficient label colliding with a variable name**, the case #376 fixed for `lda`, `qda`, `fda`, `sda` and `ksvm`. The formula method names each dummy column after the variable plus the level, so a level `y2` of `g` produces `gy2`, duplicating the predictor `gy2` in `col_names`. Max abs diff 0.84. This was unverifiable at the time of #376 because that report went through the matrix interface, where `sparsediscrim` itself errors; the formula interface fits and its `predict()` works, which makes the disagreement measurable.
4. **`sda` and `sparsediscrim` accept an ordered factor through parsnip and get it wrong.** The `contr.poly` columns `f.L` and `f.Q` are read as levels of `f`, and the generated formula compares `f` against names that never match. Max abs diff 0.79 and 0.49. `lda`, `qda` and `fda` reject the same fit.
5. **`mixOmics` through parsnip is wrong for an ordered factor** (max abs diff 1.34) and **errors on an unused factor level**: the constant dummy column gets an `NA` loading, `predict()` copes, but `tidypredict_fit()` fails with `missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed` from the `coef == 0` test that drops zero terms.
6. **`mixOmics` disagrees with `predict()` on newdata containing `NA`.** `predict.mixo_pls()` fills the missing predictor in rather than propagating it, returning a number where the generated formula returns `NA`.

## Cases that are not defects

- `MASS::lda()` and `MASS::qda()` refuse to fit a factor with an unused level ("constant within groups", "rank deficiency in group"), so that case does not reach the parser.
- `klaR::NaiveBayes()` refuses to fit on training data containing `NA` or on a zero-variance predictor.
- `mixOmics::pls()` refuses a single-column `X`, a constant outcome, and duplicated column names.
- `kernlab::ksvm()` finds no support vectors for a constant outcome; `LiblineaR` refuses a single-class outcome.
- `mda::fda()` and `MASS::lda()` return `NA` predictions for a rank-deficient fit and the generated formula returns `NA` too, so there is nothing to assert beyond agreement on `NA`.
- Both naive Bayes engines, `nullmodel`, and `sparsediscrim`'s own formula method handle every awkward factor level correctly, since they key on the level rather than on a model matrix column name.
